items.title: The Sunni-Shia split began over political succession in 632 CE
items.claim: What is the origin of the Sunni-Shia division?

options.text: Two separate communities formed centuries apart in different countries

After Muhammad's death on 8 June 632 CE without a clear successor, those who supported Abu Bakr (chosen as first caliph) became Sunni; those who held Ali (Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law) had been designated became Shia — entrenched after Husayn's martyrdom at Karbala in 680 CE

items.reveal:
Abu Bakr was chosen at Saqifah immediately after Muhammad's death. Umar (634-644), Uthman (644-656), then Ali (656-661) followed as the 'Rightly-Guided Caliphs'. Umar and Uthman were assassinated.

The First Fitna (civil war, 656-661) and Husayn ibn Ali's death at Karbala on 10 Muharram 61 AH (10 October 680 CE) crystallised Shia identity. Husayn's grandfather was Muhammad; his death is mourned annually at Ashura.

Globally, around 85-90% of Muslims are Sunni, 10-15% Shia. Shia majorities: Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Bahrain. Significant minorities: Lebanon, Yemen, Pakistan, Afghanistan, India.
items.why: Major religious traditions can be shaped by political beginnings. The Sunni-Shia distinction is real and consequential — and originally a question about who should lead, not what to believe.

items.title: Pesach commemorates the Exodus from Egypt

options.text: The giving of the Torah at Sinai
The Exodus from Egyptian slavery — the angel of death 'passing over' Jewish homes marked with lamb's blood, the hasty departure (unleavened bread, matzah), the crossing of the Red Sea
The destruction of the Second Temple

items.reveal:
Pesach falls on 15 Nisan (March-April). It lasts 7 days in Israel (and for Reform Jews worldwide), 8 days in the Diaspora for Orthodox and Conservative Jews.

The Seder is the ritual meal on the first night (and second night in the Diaspora). The Haggadah ('the telling') is recited — recounting the Exodus through symbolic foods (matzah, maror, charoset), four cups of wine, and the four questions (asked by the youngest).

The festival ends with 'Next year in Jerusalem'. Its liberation theme has shaped social movements: African American spirituals (Go Down Moses), the Civil Rights movement (King invoked Exodus), Latin American liberation theology.
items.why: Judaism's major festivals carry specific historical content. Pesach is not generic 'spring festival' but structured ritual recreation of a specific liberation narrative — central to Jewish identity for over two millennia.

items.title: Jihad means 'struggle' — and has a greater inner meaning
items.claim: What is the classical Islamic distinction between greater and lesser jihad?

options.text: Greater jihad is large-scale war; lesser jihad is small skirmishes

A widely cited hadith distinguishes the 'lesser jihad' (armed struggle in defence of the community) from the 'greater jihad' (the inner struggle against one's own ego) — though the hadith's authenticity is debated by some scholars
Jihad means only armed warfare; it has no inner meaning
Jihad refers only to economic struggle

items.reveal:
The Arabic root j-h-d means 'to strive, to exert effort'. The greater/lesser distinction is attributed to a hadith reported by al-Bayhaqi and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi: 'We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the jihad against the self.'

Scholars including Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) and modern critics question the hadith's authenticity. But the inner-struggle understanding is found independently in Sufi traditions and in mainstream piety.

Classical Islamic law (fiqh) regulates armed jihad with conditions on declaration, conduct, and protection of non-combatants — distinct from later extremist appropriations.
items.why: A word picked up by 21st-century media can carry meanings that don't match its theological tradition. 'Jihad' in classical Islam is far more various than its English-language press usage.
